ei-foundations.title: Lecture: Why emotional intelligence matters at work
ei-foundations.text: A skill, not a personality type It shapes how you handle pressure, feedback and conflict Anyone can improve it with practice. Emotional intelligence is the ability to notice emotion, understand what it is telling you, and choose a useful response. People often mistake it for being nice, or for staying calm all the time. It is neither of those. It is a set of habits. Because it is a skill and not a personality type, anyone can get better at it. In this lecture we will cover what emotional intelligence is and is not, how to spot your own patterns, a simple routine for pressure, and how to read a room more accurately.

ei-foundations.title: Lecture: What it is, and what it is not
ei-foundations.text: It is noticing, understanding and choosing It is not suppressing feelings It is not the same as being agreeable. Start with what it is not. It is not hiding what you feel, and it is not agreeing with everyone to keep the peace. Someone can be highly emotionally intelligent and still disagree firmly. What matters is that they notice what is going on inside them, understand why, and then decide how to act, instead of being driven by the first reaction. Think of it as adding a short gap between feeling something and doing something. That gap is where good judgement lives, and it is the gap we will work on throughout this course.

ei-foundations.title: Lecture: The four parts of emotional intelligence
ei-foundations.text: Self-awareness: noticing your own emotions Self-management: choosing your response Social awareness: reading other people Relationship skills: acting on what you read. A useful way to organise the skill is in four parts. Self-awareness is noticing your own emotions as they happen. Self-management is choosing how you respond rather than reacting. Social awareness is reading what other people are feeling, from their words and their body language. Relationship skills are using all of that to communicate, give feedback and resolve disagreement. The parts build on each other. If you cannot notice your own frustration, you will struggle to manage it, and you will probably miss the same feeling in the person across the table.

ei-foundations.title: Lecture: Mapping your triggers
ei-foundations.text: Triggers follow patterns Note the situation, the person and the time of day Name the feeling in one word. Most reactive moments are not random. They follow a pattern. A certain kind of email, a certain person interrupting, the end of a long day. The first practical step is to map your triggers. For one week, whenever you feel pulled off balance, write down three things: what happened, who was involved, and the time of day. Then name the feeling in a single word, such as irritated, anxious or dismissed. Naming it matters, because a named feeling is easier to manage than a vague one. After a week, look for repeats.

ei-foundations.title: Lecture: The ninety second pause
ei-foundations.text: Breathe Name the feeling Decide the next useful step. Once you know your triggers, you need something to do in the moment. The ninety second pause is a short, repeatable routine for the gap between a trigger and your response. First, breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in. Second, name the feeling to yourself in one word. Third, decide the next useful step, which might be answering, asking a question, or saying that you will come back to it. It sounds almost too simple. That is the point. Under pressure you will not remember a complicated method, but you can remember three steps.

ei-foundations.title: Lecture: Reading the room
ei-foundations.text: Notice who is speaking and who is quiet Watch for changes in tone and pace Check your read with a question. Reading the room means noticing the signals other people give off, and adjusting how you contribute so your point lands. In a meeting, notice who is speaking a lot and who has gone quiet. Notice when the pace or tone changes, or when someone looks away. These are signals, not proof. So check your read with a question, such as, it seems like there are some concerns, what are we missing. Asking is better than assuming. Over time, this habit makes you the person who senses a problem early, instead of the one surprised by it.

ei-foundations.title: Lecture: Putting it together on a normal Tuesday
ei-foundations.text: Trigger, then pause, then choice Practise on small moments first Review once a week. Here is how the pieces fit on an ordinary day. A message arrives that annoys you. You notice the tightness, which is self-awareness. You take your ninety second pause, which is self-management. Before you reply, you think about what the sender might be dealing with, which is social awareness. Then you write a reply that gets the result you want, which is a relationship skill. Practise on small moments first, not the hardest conversation of the year. And once a week, spend ten minutes reviewing which triggers showed up and how you handled them.

ei-foundations.title: Lecture: Your next steps
ei-foundations.text: Pick one trigger to work on this week Use the pause three times Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, choose one trigger from your map and commit to using the pause the next three times it appears. Do not try to fix everything at once. Open the workbook for this course and complete the exercises, because writing things down makes them stick. Then take the final quiz, which checks the main ideas from every phase. When you finish the last lesson, you will receive your certificate and a short personal review of how you worked through the course. Thank you for listening, and good luck putting this into practice.

ei-foundations.title: Glossary: Emotional intelligence
ei-foundations.text: Emotional intelligence: The ability to notice emotion, understand what it is telling you and choose a useful response.

ei-foundations.title: Glossary: Trigger
ei-foundations.text: Trigger: A situation, person or moment that reliably pulls you off balance.

ei-foundations.title: Glossary: Self-awareness
ei-foundations.text: Self-awareness: Noticing your own emotions and reactions as they happen.

ei-foundations.title: Glossary: Ninety second pause
ei-foundations.text: Ninety second pause: A three-step routine for the gap between a trigger and your response: breathe, name the feeling, decide the next step.

ei-foundations.title: Exercise: Seven-day trigger log
ei-foundations.text: Each time you feel pulled off balance, write what happened, who was involved and the time of day. Name the feeling in a single word. Use the ninety second pause and note what you did next. At the end of the week, circle the pattern that appeared most often.

ei-foundations.title: Reflection questions
ei-foundations.text: Which situation at work most often pulls you off balance, and what does that reaction look like from the outside? When did you last choose your response instead of reacting, and what made that possible? Who in your team is hardest to read, and what question could you ask to check your read?

first-time-manager.title: Lecture: The shift from doing to leading
first-time-manager.text: Your job is now other people's results Your attention is the scarce resource Let go of the right things first. Welcome to The First-Time Manager. The biggest change in your first year is not a new title, it is a new job. You used to be measured on your own work. Now you are measured on what your team achieves. That shift is mostly about where you spend your attention. Many new managers keep doing the work they were good at, because it feels safe, and then have no time left to lead. In this lecture we cover one to ones, delegation and feedback, which are the three habits that make the first year work.

first-time-manager.title: Lecture: What to let go of first
first-time-manager.text: Tasks others can learn to do The need to be the expert Being available for everything. Letting go is hard because the tasks you drop are often the ones you do best. Start with work that someone else can learn, even if they will do it slower at first. Let go of needing to be the expert in the room, because your value now is helping others do well. And let go of being available for every question, since constant interruptions teach people to depend on you. A useful test is to ask whether a task needs you specifically, or just needs to get done. If it is the second, it is a candidate for handing over.

first-time-manager.title: Lecture: One to ones that matter
first-time-manager.text: Weekly, short, and about them Start with their agenda Surface problems early. A good one to one is the most useful management tool you have. Keep it weekly and keep it regular, even when it is short. Make it about the other person, not a status update for you. Start by asking what they would like to talk about, then cover what is blocking them, what they are proud of, and what support they need. The aim is to surface problems early, while they are still small. If you cancel one to ones when you are busy, people learn that they come second, and they stop bringing you the early warnings.

first-time-manager.title: Lecture: A simple one to one structure
first-time-manager.text: Check in as a person Their topics, then yours Agree actions and write them down. Here is a structure you can use straight away. Begin with a short check in, how are things, really. Then cover their topics first, followed by yours. Ask open questions such as, what would make this week easier. Before you finish, agree on actions, who will do what by when, and write them down so you can start the next meeting by reviewing them. Keep notes brief and keep them private. Over a few weeks the pattern builds trust, because people can see that what they say leads to something happening.

first-time-manager.title: Lecture: Delegation without disappearing
first-time-manager.text: Match support to the person and the task Share the outcome and the why Agree check-ins before you hand over. Delegation does not mean throwing a task over the wall. Match the level of support to the person and the task. Someone new to a task needs more guidance than someone who has done it five times. Share the outcome you want and the reason it matters, not only the steps. And agree check-ins before you hand anything over, so that you stay informed without hovering. Delegating and disappearing leaves people stuck. Delegating and hovering takes the ownership back. The middle path is clear expectations, agreed checkpoints, and trust between them.

first-time-manager.title: Lecture: Feedback that lands
first-time-manager.text: Describe the behaviour Explain its impact Say what you would like instead, then listen. Feedback works best when it is specific and timely. Describe the behaviour you saw, without judging the person. Explain the impact it had on the team or the result. Say what you would like to see instead. Then stop talking and listen, because the other person may know something you do not. Give positive feedback with the same care, since people repeat what they are told works. Do not save feedback for the annual review. A small comment given the same week is easier to hear and easier to act on than a large one given months later.

first-time-manager.title: Lecture: Common mistakes in the first year
first-time-manager.text: Avoiding the hard conversation Treating everyone the same way Forgetting to ask for feedback yourself. Three mistakes appear again and again. The first is avoiding the hard conversation, hoping it will fix itself. It rarely does, and the problem usually grows. The second is treating everyone the same, when people need different levels of support and different ways of hearing feedback. The third is forgetting to ask for feedback yourself. Ask your team what you could do differently, and then actually do something with the answer. Being willing to hear it models the behaviour you want from them, and it shows you are still learning too.

first-time-manager.title: Lecture: Your next steps
first-time-manager.text: Book your next three one to ones Choose one task to delegate this week Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, put your next three one to ones in the diary now. Choose one task you will delegate this week, and write down the outcome, the reason, and the check in date. Complete the workbook for this course, which has templates for each habit. Then take the final quiz. When you reach the end of the last lesson you will receive your certificate and a personal review of how you completed the course. The first year is demanding, so be patient with yourself, and keep practising these three habits.

first-time-manager.title: Glossary: One to one
first-time-manager.text: One to one: A regular private meeting between a manager and a team member, centred on the team member.

first-time-manager.title: Glossary: Delegation
first-time-manager.text: Delegation: Handing over a task with clear expectations, support and agreed check-ins.

first-time-manager.title: Glossary: Feedback
first-time-manager.text: Feedback: Specific information about behaviour and its impact, with a suggestion for what to do instead.

first-time-manager.title: Glossary: Check-in
first-time-manager.text: Check-in: A planned point at which you review progress on delegated work.

first-time-manager.title: Exercise: Delegation plan
first-time-manager.text: Pick one task you could hand over this week. Write the outcome you want and why it matters. Decide the support the person needs and two check-in dates. Hand it over and review it at the first check-in.

first-time-manager.title: Reflection questions
first-time-manager.text: Which task are you still doing that someone else could learn, and what is stopping you handing it over? When did you last leave a one to one with an action that actually happened? What feedback have you been avoiding giving, and what would the useful version sound like?

leading-through-change.title: Lecture: Change from the team's point of view
leading-through-change.text: Change is usually done to people Uncertainty feels like a threat Resistance is information. Welcome to Leading Through Change. When an organisation changes, leaders often see an opportunity, while the people affected see uncertainty. They wonder what happens to their role, their routine and their team. That difference in view explains most of the friction. In this lecture we will look at why people resist change, how to explain the reason for it in plain language, how to spot resistance early, and how to keep momentum going after the launch, which is where many programmes quietly fade.

leading-through-change.title: Lecture: Why people resist change
leading-through-change.text: They expect to lose something They do not understand the reason They doubt it will be seen through. Resistance is usually information. People resist when they expect to lose something, such as status, familiar routines or relationships. They resist when they do not understand why the change is happening, so it feels arbitrary. And they resist when they have seen earlier changes started and abandoned, so they doubt this one will last. If you treat resistance as an attitude problem, you will argue. If you treat it as information, you will ask what the person expects to lose, and that is a far more useful conversation.

leading-through-change.title: Lecture: Talking about loss honestly
leading-through-change.text: Name what will change Name what will stay the same Do not pretend there is no cost. Being honest about loss builds credibility. If a team will lose a familiar process, say so. If some roles will look different, say so. People can cope with bad news far better than with the sense that something is being hidden. Equally important is saying what will not change, because that gives people something stable to stand on. Avoid selling the change as purely positive. A balanced message, this will be harder for a while, here is why it is worth it, and here is how we will support you, is both truthful and reassuring.

leading-through-change.title: Lecture: The change story
leading-through-change.text: Where we are Where we are going and why What will not change. A change story is a short, honest narrative that you can repeat. It has three parts. First, where we are now, including what is not working. Second, where we are going and why, in plain language a new starter would understand. Third, what will not change, such as your values or your commitment to people. Write it in a few sentences, test it on someone outside the project, and remove any jargon. A good test is whether a team member could retell it to a colleague after hearing it once. If they cannot, simplify it.

leading-through-change.title: Lecture: Spotting resistance early
leading-through-change.text: Silence in meetings Quiet workarounds Questions that circle back to the old way. Resistance rarely announces itself. Look for silence in meetings where you expected questions. Look for quiet workarounds, where people keep using the old process alongside the new one. Notice questions that keep returning to how things used to work. When you see these signs, do not push harder. Ask openly, what is making this difficult, and listen without defending. Often the problem is practical, a missing tool, a gap in training, or an unclear role. Fixing a practical barrier early is much cheaper than overcoming a hardened position later.

leading-through-change.title: Lecture: Keeping momentum after launch
leading-through-change.text: Make progress visible Celebrate small wins Build short regular check-ins. Most change efforts fade after the launch. Energy drops, attention moves on, and old habits return. To keep momentum, make progress visible. A simple board or a short update each week shows people that the change is real. Celebrate small wins, because they prove the direction is right. And build regular check-ins into the calendar where people can say what is working and what is not. Small rituals, repeated, do more than a big launch event. The goal is for the new way to become the normal way, and that takes repetition.

leading-through-change.title: Lecture: Your role as the leader
leading-through-change.text: Be consistent in what you say and do Stay visible during the hard weeks Ask for feedback and act on it. People watch what leaders do more closely than what they say. If you announce a new way of working and then use the old one yourself, the message is lost. Be consistent. Stay visible during the difficult weeks, rather than disappearing once the plan is approved. And ask for feedback on how the change is landing, then visibly act on at least some of it. When people see that their input changes something, they move from watching the change to taking part in it. That shift is what turns compliance into commitment.

leading-through-change.title: Lecture: Your next steps
leading-through-change.text: Write your change story in five sentences List the likely losses and your response Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, write your change story in no more than five sentences and test it on one person. List the losses your team may feel and how you will respond to each. Complete the workbook for this course, which has a template for the change story and a resistance map. Then take the final quiz. When you finish the last lesson, you will receive your certificate and a personal review of your progress. Change is hard for everyone involved, and your steadiness as a leader makes a real difference.

leading-through-change.title: Glossary: Resistance
leading-through-change.text: Resistance: A response to change that signals an expected loss, a lack of understanding or a lack of trust.

leading-through-change.title: Glossary: Change story
leading-through-change.text: Change story: A short honest narrative covering where we are, where we are going and what will not change.

leading-through-change.title: Glossary: Workaround
leading-through-change.text: Workaround: A way of doing something that quietly avoids the new process.

leading-through-change.title: Glossary: Momentum
leading-through-change.text: Momentum: The sense that progress is real and continuing after the launch.

leading-through-change.title: Exercise: Resistance map
leading-through-change.text: List the people or groups affected by your change. For each, write what they may expect to lose. Write one honest sentence you could say to each group. Choose one practical barrier to remove this week.

leading-through-change.title: Reflection questions
leading-through-change.text: Think of a change you went through. What did you expect to lose, and did anyone ask? What would your team say is the reason for the change you are leading, in their own words? Which small ritual could you add to keep the change visible every week?

team-trust-reset.title: Lecture: What trust looks like in practice
team-trust-reset.text: Trust shows up in small behaviours People say what they really think Mistakes are shared, not hidden. Welcome to Team Trust Reset. Trust can sound abstract, but in a team it shows up in small, visible behaviours. People say what they really think in meetings, not afterwards in the corridor. Mistakes are shared early, instead of hidden. People ask for help without worrying how it will look. When trust is low, all of these shrink, and the team slows down without anyone quite knowing why. This lecture covers how to recognise the signs, run a team charter session, work through tensions, and keep trust healthy with a monthly check.

team-trust-reset.title: Lecture: Psychological safety
team-trust-reset.text: The belief that you can speak up safely It is built by how leaders respond It is not the same as being comfortable. Psychological safety is the shared belief that you can speak up, ask a question or admit a mistake without being embarrassed or punished. It is built mostly by how leaders respond. If someone raises a concern and gets a sharp reply, the whole team notices and stays quiet. If they get thanks, the team notices that too. Psychological safety is not the same as being comfortable. A safe team can still disagree strongly, because people trust that the disagreement is about the work, not about them.

team-trust-reset.title: Lecture: Signs that trust has dropped
team-trust-reset.text: Meetings with little discussion Decisions revisited after the meeting Blame when something goes wrong. Look for the signs. Meetings where nobody disagrees and then people complain afterwards. Decisions that are agreed in the room and quietly reopened later. A habit of finding who is to blame when something goes wrong, rather than what can be learned. People checking and double checking each other's work. None of these mean the team is bad. They mean that people do not feel safe being open. Spotting the pattern early gives you a chance to address it before it becomes the way the team works.

team-trust-reset.title: Lecture: Writing a team charter
team-trust-reset.text: Agree how you will work together Keep it short and in your own words Make it visible and review it. A team charter is a short agreement on how you will work together. It covers things like how you give feedback, how you make decisions, how quickly you reply, and what you do when you disagree. Run it as a session where everyone contributes, rather than something the manager writes alone. Keep the language simple and use the team's own words. Then make it visible, on a shared page or at the start of meetings, and review it every few months. A charter that lives in a drawer changes nothing.

team-trust-reset.title: Lecture: Running the session
team-trust-reset.text: Start with what works well already Collect ideas individually first Agree three to five commitments. To run the charter session, start by asking what already works well, so the conversation begins from strength. Let people write their ideas individually before sharing, so that quieter members are not drowned out. Group the ideas into themes, then agree on three to five commitments that everyone can actually keep. More than that, and nobody remembers them. End by deciding how you will remind each other, and when you will review. The conversation matters as much as the document, because that is where people learn what others expect.

team-trust-reset.title: Lecture: Working through team tensions
team-trust-reset.text: Name the tension without blaming Separate the issue from the person Agree one small change to try. Every team has tensions. The aim is not to remove them but to work through them. Name the tension in neutral terms, for example, we seem to have different views on how fast to move. Separate the issue from the person, so that it does not become personal. Ask each side what matters most to them. Then agree one small change to try for two weeks, and review it. Small experiments are easier to agree to than large demands, and they build the habit of resolving things instead of avoiding them.

team-trust-reset.title: Lecture: The monthly team health check
team-trust-reset.text: Three questions: trust, clarity, energy Anonymous scores and open discussion One action each month. A monthly health check keeps trust from drifting. Ask three simple questions. How much do we trust each other to be open. How clear are we on our goals and roles. How is our energy. Collect scores anonymously, then discuss the results together. Do not try to fix everything. Choose one action for the month and write down who owns it. Over time, you will see the scores move, and you will have a record of what worked. Consistency matters more than sophistication, so keep it short and keep it regular.

team-trust-reset.title: Lecture: Your next steps
team-trust-reset.text: Schedule your charter session Draft your three health check questions Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, book a charter session with your team in the next two weeks. Draft the three questions for your first health check and decide how you will collect the answers. Complete the workbook for this course, which has a charter template and a health check form. Then take the final quiz. When you reach the end of the last lesson you will receive your certificate and a personal review. Trust is rebuilt mostly through small kept promises, so start with one you can keep this week.

team-trust-reset.title: Glossary: Psychological safety
team-trust-reset.text: Psychological safety: The shared belief that you can speak up, ask or admit a mistake without being embarrassed or punished.

team-trust-reset.title: Glossary: Team charter
team-trust-reset.text: Team charter: A short agreement on how the team will work together, made by the team and reviewed regularly.

team-trust-reset.title: Glossary: Team health check
team-trust-reset.text: Team health check: A short regular survey of trust, clarity and energy, followed by one action.

team-trust-reset.title: Glossary: Tension
team-trust-reset.text: Tension: A difference in views or needs that, if unspoken, affects how the team works.

team-trust-reset.title: Exercise: Draft a team charter
team-trust-reset.text: List three behaviours you want more of in the team. List three you want less of. Turn them into three to five commitments in the team's own words. Agree where the charter will live and when you will review it.

team-trust-reset.title: Reflection questions
team-trust-reset.text: When did someone in your team last disagree openly, and how was it received? Which team agreement is most often broken, and what would make it easier to keep? What is one small promise you could keep this week that your team would notice?

sustainable-performance.title: Lecture: Performance depends on recovery
sustainable-performance.text: Effort without recovery does not last Energy is the real resource Sustainable beats heroic. Welcome to Sustainable Performance. Many people believe that doing well means working longer. In practice, output depends on energy as much as on hours. Effort without recovery works for a short sprint, but it wears people down over months. This lecture is about doing good work in a way you can keep up. We will cover how to plan around energy, how to set boundaries you can keep, how to notice overload early, and how to build small recovery habits into an ordinary week.

sustainable-performance.title: Lecture: Energy is the real resource
sustainable-performance.text: Time is fixed, energy is not Notice when you do your best thinking Protect that time for important work. You cannot add hours to the day, but you can change how much energy you bring to them. Most people have a pattern. Some think best early, others in the afternoon. Spend a week noticing when your focus is sharpest and when it dips. Then protect your best hours for work that needs real thought, and use the low-energy times for routine tasks like admin and email. Planning your week around energy, not just time, often gets more done in fewer hours, and leaves you less drained at the end of the day.

sustainable-performance.title: Lecture: Four kinds of energy
sustainable-performance.text: Physical: sleep, movement, food Emotional: how you feel Mental: focus and attention Purpose: why the work matters. It helps to think of energy in four kinds. Physical energy comes from sleep, movement and food, and it underpins everything else. Emotional energy is how you feel, which is affected by relationships and by stress. Mental energy is focus, and it is drained by constant switching between tasks. Purpose energy comes from knowing why your work matters. When you feel flat, ask which of the four is low. The answer points to a different fix each time. A short walk helps physical energy, while a clearer goal helps purpose.

sustainable-performance.title: Lecture: Boundaries you can keep
sustainable-performance.text: A boundary is a clear, kind limit Offer an alternative where you can Start with one you can actually hold. A boundary is a clear, kind limit on what you will do and when. It is not a refusal to help. A healthy boundary often sounds like, I can do that on Thursday, or, I can do the first half today. Offering an alternative keeps the relationship positive. The common mistake is setting a boundary so ambitious that you break it within days, which teaches you to ignore your own limits. Start with one that you can actually hold, such as not checking messages after a set time, and build from there.

sustainable-performance.title: Lecture: Recognising overload early
sustainable-performance.text: Trouble switching off Irritability and cynicism Small tasks feel heavy. Overload builds slowly, so the early signs are easy to miss. Watch for trouble switching off in the evening, a shorter temper, a growing cynicism about work, or small tasks that suddenly feel heavy. Changes in sleep and appetite are also common signals. The key is to notice the trend, not a single bad day. If you see several signs for more than a couple of weeks, treat it as information and act. Talk to someone, reduce a commitment, or ask for support. Waiting until you are exhausted makes recovery much longer.

sustainable-performance.title: Lecture: Small recovery habits
sustainable-performance.text: Short breaks between demanding tasks A real end to the working day One thing each week that restores you. Recovery does not have to mean a holiday. Short breaks between demanding tasks let your attention reset. A clear end to the working day, such as closing the laptop and taking a short walk, helps your mind switch off. And one thing each week that genuinely restores you, whether that is exercise, time with friends, or a hobby, gives you something to look forward to. These habits are small, but they add up. The key is to schedule them like meetings, because if they are optional, they are the first thing to go.

sustainable-performance.title: Lecture: Talking about workload
sustainable-performance.text: Be specific about what is on your plate Ask what can wait Raise it early, with options. If your workload is too high, saying so early is a strength, not a weakness. Be specific. Instead of saying you are overwhelmed, list what is on your plate and what each item needs. Ask your manager or colleague what can wait or be dropped. Bring options rather than only a problem, such as moving a deadline or sharing a task. Most managers prefer to hear about pressure when there is still room to adjust. Keeping quiet until something breaks is harder for everyone, including you.

sustainable-performance.title: Lecture: Your next steps
sustainable-performance.text: Track your energy for one week Choose one boundary to hold Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, track your energy levels for one week, noting when you feel sharp and when you feel flat. Choose one boundary that you will hold, and tell someone about it. Complete the workbook for this course, which includes an energy log and a weekly planning page. Then take the final quiz. When you reach the end of the last lesson you will receive your certificate and a personal review of how you worked through the course. Sustainable performance is built from small, steady habits, so be patient and keep going.

sustainable-performance.title: Glossary: Energy
sustainable-performance.text: Energy: The capacity you bring to work: physical, emotional, mental and purpose-related.

sustainable-performance.title: Glossary: Boundary
sustainable-performance.text: Boundary: A clear, kind limit on what you will do and when.

sustainable-performance.title: Glossary: Overload
sustainable-performance.text: Overload: A sustained state where demands exceed your capacity to recover.

sustainable-performance.title: Glossary: Recovery
sustainable-performance.text: Recovery: Activities that restore energy, from short breaks to rest days.

sustainable-performance.title: Exercise: One-week energy log
sustainable-performance.text: Three times a day, rate your energy from one to five. Note what you were doing and what you had eaten or slept. At the end of the week, mark your two best hours of the day. Move one important task into those hours next week.

sustainable-performance.title: Reflection questions
sustainable-performance.text: At what time of day do you do your best thinking, and how much of that time is protected? Which boundary have you set and broken, and what would a more realistic version look like? What are your first two signs of overload, and who could you tell?

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Lecture: Why managers have well-being conversations
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: You see changes early People often will not raise it first Your role is to listen and signpost. Welcome to Well-being Conversations for Managers. Managers are often the first to notice when someone is struggling. A change in mood, in quality of work, or in attendance can all be signals. Many people will not raise a problem themselves, because they worry how it will look. A short, kind conversation can make a real difference. This lecture covers how to open the conversation, how to listen without trying to fix, how to know your limits, and how to point people to the right support.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Lecture: Your role and its limits
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: You are not a therapist You are not expected to diagnose You can listen, support and signpost. It is important to be clear about your role. You are not a therapist or a doctor, and you are not expected to diagnose anything. What you can do is notice, ask, listen and point towards help. Knowing this takes pressure off. You do not need to have the answers. You need to be willing to have the conversation, to take it seriously, and to follow up. That mix of care and clear limits protects both the person and you, and it keeps the conversation useful rather than awkward.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Lecture: Opening the conversation
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: Choose a private, unhurried moment Start with what you have noticed Ask an open question. Choose a private, unhurried moment, not the end of a busy meeting. Start with what you have noticed, in neutral terms, for example, I have noticed you have seemed quieter lately. Then ask an open question, such as, how are things, really. Avoid questions that push for an answer, like, what is wrong with you. Make it clear that there is no pressure to share. Some people will talk straight away, and others will not. Saying that the door is open, and following up later, is often what makes the next conversation easier.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Lecture: Listening without fixing
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: Let them finish Reflect back what you heard Resist offering solutions straight away. The instinct of many managers is to jump to solutions. In a well-being conversation, that can feel dismissive. Instead, let the person finish. Reflect back what you heard, for example, it sounds like the workload has been weighing on you. Ask whether they would like advice, or just to be heard. Silence is fine. When people feel listened to, they often work out their own next step. If a practical change is needed, such as adjusting a deadline, you can agree it together once they have said what they need.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Lecture: Useful phrases and ones to avoid
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: Helpful: that sounds hard, thank you for telling me Avoid: I know exactly how you feel Avoid: just try to stay positive. Language matters. Helpful phrases include, that sounds really hard, thank you for telling me, and, what would help right now. Phrases to avoid include, I know exactly how you feel, because you probably do not. Also avoid, just try to stay positive, and, other people have it worse. These shut the conversation down. Keep your tone steady and unhurried. You do not have to say the perfect thing. A genuine, simple response, such as, I am glad you told me, is usually enough to show you care.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Lecture: Knowing your limits
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: Do not promise confidentiality you cannot keep Know when to involve others Take immediate risk seriously. Be honest about what you can promise. You should not promise absolute confidentiality, because if there is a risk to someone's safety, you may need to involve others. Say what you can keep private and when you would need to share. Know your organisation's process and who to contact, such as HR or an employee assistance line. If someone is in immediate danger or mentions harming themselves, treat it as urgent and follow your emergency procedures. Knowing your limits is part of caring for the person well.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Lecture: Signposting and following up
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: Know the support available Offer, do not push Check in again within a week. Signposting means pointing someone to the right support. Learn what your organisation offers, such as counselling, an employee assistance programme, or occupational health, and also what external services exist. Offer the information and let the person choose. Then follow up. A short check in within a week, how are you doing, shows that the first conversation was not a one-off. Keep a brief private note of what you agreed. Following up is often the most valued part, because it shows that you meant what you said.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Lecture: Your next steps
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: Find your organisation's support options Prepare an opening you are comfortable with Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, find out what support your organisation offers, and write down the contact details so you have them ready. Prepare an opening sentence for a well-being conversation that feels natural in your own words. Complete the workbook for this course, which includes a conversation guide and a follow up planner. Then take the final quiz. When you reach the end of the last lesson you will receive your certificate and a personal review. These conversations get easier with practice, and your willingness to start them matters.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Glossary: Signposting
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: Signposting: Pointing someone to appropriate support without taking on the role of counsellor.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Glossary: Open question
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: Open question: A question that invites more than a yes or no answer, such as "how are things, really?"

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Glossary: Reflective listening
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: Reflective listening: Repeating back what you heard in your own words to show you understood.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Glossary: Employee assistance programme
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: Employee assistance programme: A confidential support service some employers provide for staff.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Exercise: Conversation plan
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: Write an opening sentence that mentions what you noticed, in neutral terms. Write two open questions you could ask. List the support options you could signpost to. Plan when you will check in again.

manager-wellbeing-conversations.title: Reflection questions
manager-wellbeing-conversations.text: What stops you from asking someone how they are, really? When someone shares a problem, do you tend to fix it or listen, and what is the effect? Who in your organisation could you contact if someone needed more support than you can give?

ei-in-practice.title: Lecture: Emotions in everyday decisions
ei-in-practice.text: Emotion is data, not noise Unnoticed feelings steer decisions Name it, then decide. Welcome to Emotional Intelligence in Practice. This course assumes you know the basics, and focuses on using them in real situations: decisions, feedback and conflict. We start with the idea that emotions are data, not noise. A feeling of unease before a meeting may be pointing at something real. A feeling of excitement may be clouding your judgement. Unnoticed feelings steer decisions quietly. When you notice and name them, you can take them into account without letting them take over.

ei-in-practice.title: Lecture: Reading your emotional signals
ei-in-practice.text: Notice the body first Ask what the feeling is about Decide whether it helps this decision. Emotions often show up in the body before the mind. A tight chest, a clenched jaw, a knot in the stomach. Learn your own early signals. When you feel one, ask what it is about. Is it the situation, the person, or something older that the situation reminds you of. Then ask whether the feeling helps with the decision in front of you. Sometimes it does, for instance caution before a risky move. Sometimes it does not, such as irritation about something unrelated. Sorting the two is a skill that improves with use.

ei-in-practice.title: Lecture: Staying steady in a heated conversation
ei-in-practice.text: Slow your breathing and your pace Name the emotion in the room Return to the shared goal. When a conversation heats up, the first job is to steady yourself. Slow your breathing and slow your speech, because your pace sets the pace for everyone. If the emotion is obvious, name it calmly, for example, I can see this matters a lot to both of us. Then return to the shared goal, which is usually a good result for the team or the customer. Avoid arguing about who is right. The aim is not to win the point, it is to reach a solution you can both live with, while keeping the relationship intact.

ei-in-practice.title: Lecture: Feedback without the sting
ei-in-practice.text: Be specific about the behaviour Describe the impact, not the character Invite their view. Feedback often triggers defensiveness because it feels like a judgement of the person. To reduce that, describe the specific behaviour, not a trait. Say, in the last two meetings you interrupted before others finished, not, you are rude. Describe the impact, for example, the team has stopped sharing ideas. Then invite their view, since they may have context you lack. Defensiveness drops when people feel heard. If you are receiving feedback, listen fully first, thank the person, and take time before responding if you need it.

ei-in-practice.title: Lecture: Working through conflict
ei-in-practice.text: Make both sides feel heard Separate interests from positions Agree a next step. Conflict is normal in any team that cares about its work. The first goal is to make both sides feel heard, which often reduces the heat by itself. Next, separate positions from interests. A position is what someone says they want. An interest is why they want it. Two people may disagree on the position but share the interest, such as a smooth launch. Once interests are on the table, options appear. Finish by agreeing a concrete next step, and a time to check whether it worked.

ei-in-practice.title: Lecture: Influencing without authority
ei-in-practice.text: Understand what the other person cares about Make a clear, specific request Build trust before you need it. Much of working life involves influencing people who do not report to you. Start by understanding what they care about, and connect your request to it. Make the request clear and specific, including what you need, by when, and why. And build trust before you need it, by being reliable and helping others when you can. People are far more willing to support someone they trust. Avoid pressure tactics, which may work once, but damage the relationship. Respect and clarity are slower, but they last.

ei-in-practice.title: Lecture: Putting it into practice
ei-in-practice.text: Choose one conversation you have been avoiding Prepare the opening and the goal Review how it went afterwards. The way to build these skills is to use them on real conversations. Choose one you have been avoiding. Prepare how you will open, what the shared goal is, and what you will do if the other person becomes upset. Have the conversation, then review. What went well, what would you change, what did you learn about the other person. Writing a few lines straight afterwards makes the learning stick. Each conversation makes the next one easier, and over a few months the change in how you handle difficult moments becomes clear.

ei-in-practice.title: Lecture: Your next steps
ei-in-practice.text: Pick one conversation to have this week Use the feedback structure Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, pick one conversation you will have this week and write down your opening. Use the feedback structure from this lecture. Complete the workbook for this course, which has a conflict planning sheet and a feedback template. Then take the final quiz. When you reach the end of the last lesson, you will receive your certificate and a personal review of how you worked through the course. Thank you for your time, and good luck with the conversations ahead.

ei-in-practice.title: Glossary: Position
ei-in-practice.text: Position: What someone says they want in a disagreement.

ei-in-practice.title: Glossary: Interest
ei-in-practice.text: Interest: The reason behind a position, which often overlaps with what the other side wants.

ei-in-practice.title: Glossary: Defensiveness
ei-in-practice.text: Defensiveness: A protective reaction to perceived criticism that makes listening harder.

ei-in-practice.title: Glossary: Influence
ei-in-practice.text: Influence: Moving a decision or action without relying on formal authority.

ei-in-practice.title: Exercise: Prepare a difficult conversation
ei-in-practice.text: Write the shared goal in one sentence. Write your opening using behaviour, impact and an invitation. List the other person's likely interests. After the conversation, note what went well and what you would change.

ei-in-practice.title: Reflection questions
ei-in-practice.text: Which emotion tends to influence your decisions without you noticing? What is the conversation you have been putting off, and what is the shared goal in it? How do you usually react when you receive feedback, and what would you like to change?

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Lecture: Leaders set the weather
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Your mood spreads through the team People read you closely Climate affects performance. Welcome to The Emotionally Intelligent Leader. A leader's mood tends to spread through a team. People watch how you react to news, how you handle pressure, and whether you listen. Researchers describe this as the leader setting the weather. A tense leader creates a tense team, and a steady leader makes it easier for others to think clearly. This lecture covers how to read and shape the climate of your team deliberately, how to stay calm under organisational pressure, and how to coach other managers to grow their own emotional intelligence.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Lecture: Reading the climate of a team
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Listen to what is not being said Watch energy across the week Ask people directly, and often. Before you can shape the climate, you need to read it. Listen to what is not being said, such as the topics people avoid. Watch the energy across the week. When does it rise, and when does it fall. Ask people directly, in one to ones and in small groups, how things feel. Short pulse questions help, as long as you act on the answers. Keep in mind that people tell leaders less than they tell each other. So the picture you see is usually more positive than the reality. Make it easy and safe to tell you the truth.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Lecture: Shaping the climate on purpose
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Decide the tone you want Show it in small behaviours Repeat it consistently. Once you can read the climate, decide what you want it to be, such as open, focused and calm. Then show it in small behaviours. How you start meetings, how you respond to bad news, how you thank people. Small, repeated actions shape culture more than speeches. Consistency matters, because people notice when words and behaviour differ. If you say you value candour, but react badly when someone disagrees, they will believe your reaction. Aim to be predictable in the ways that matter, so people feel safe around you.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Lecture: Leading under pressure
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Pressure travels downward Pause before you pass it on Say what you know and what you do not. Pressure on a leader travels downward. If you pass on urgency without thinking, it becomes anxiety for others. Before you communicate a difficult message, pause. Ask what the team needs to know, and what is still uncertain. Then be honest about both. Saying, here is what I know, here is what I do not know yet, and here is when I will update you, creates steadiness. People cope better with uncertainty than with silence. Look after your own recovery too, because a depleted leader has less to give.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Lecture: Making it safe to speak up
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Thank people who bring bad news Respond to ideas with curiosity Admit your own mistakes. Teams perform better when people can speak up. You create that safety through your reactions. Thank people who bring bad news, even if you do not like it. Respond to ideas with curiosity, by asking questions before judging. And admit your own mistakes openly, which shows that errors can be discussed. When a leader says, I got that wrong, here is what I learned, it gives permission to others. Safety is built slowly through many small responses, and it can be damaged quickly by one careless reaction, so stay aware.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Lecture: Growing emotional intelligence in your managers
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Coach in one to ones, not memos Ask questions that build awareness Give feedback on how they lead. If you lead managers, your impact multiplies through them. Emotional intelligence grows best through coaching, not through a memo or an annual test. Use your one to ones with managers to ask questions that build awareness. How do you think the team experienced that meeting. What did you notice in yourself. Give specific feedback on how they lead, including the effect on their team. Model the behaviour yourself, since managers copy what leaders do. Encourage them to practise in small moments, and to reflect on them regularly.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Lecture: Your own development as a leader
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Ask for honest feedback Notice your patterns under stress Build a reflection habit. Leaders need development too, and often get less feedback as they become more senior. Ask for honest feedback from people you trust, and make it clear that you want the truth. Notice your own patterns under stress, such as becoming controlling or withdrawn. A short reflection habit helps. At the end of each week, note one moment you handled well, and one you would handle differently. Over time, this builds the self-awareness that everything else depends on. The best leaders stay curious about their own impact.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Lecture: Your next steps
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Choose one climate behaviour to model Plan one coaching question per manager Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, choose one behaviour that you will model consistently this month, such as how you open meetings. Write one coaching question for each manager who reports to you. Complete the workbook for this course, which includes a climate check and a reflection log. Then take the final quiz. When you reach the end of the last lesson, you will receive your certificate and a personal review of how you worked through the course. Thank you for listening, and good luck leading with awareness.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Glossary: Team climate
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Team climate: The shared feeling in a team that shapes how safe and energised people are at work.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Glossary: Pulse question
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Pulse question: A short, frequent question used to read how the team is feeling.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Glossary: Coaching
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Coaching: Helping someone build their own awareness and skill through questions and feedback.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Glossary: Modelling
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Modelling: Showing through your own behaviour the standard you expect from others.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Exercise: Climate check
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: Ask three people to describe the mood of the team in three words. Compare their answers with how you would describe it. Choose one behaviour that could shift the climate in the direction you want. Repeat the check in a month.

emotionally-intelligent-leader.title: Reflection questions
emotionally-intelligent-leader.text: How would your team describe the weather you create on a bad day? What is one behaviour of yours that people copy, for better or worse? Which manager would benefit most from a coaching conversation this month?

leadership-essentials.title: Lecture: Leadership is a behaviour
leadership-essentials.text: Leadership is what you do, not your title Anyone can lead in a moment Small behaviours add up. Welcome to Leadership Essentials. Leadership is often linked to a job title, but it is really a set of behaviours. Anyone can lead in a moment, by taking ownership of a problem, helping a colleague, or making a clear suggestion. That means you can start practising now, whatever your role. In this lecture we cover taking ownership without taking over, communicating a clear next step, and building trust through small kept promises. These are simple ideas, but they separate people others want to follow from those they simply work for.

leadership-essentials.title: Lecture: Ownership without taking over
leadership-essentials.text: Own the outcome, share the work Ask before you step in Let others do it their way. Taking ownership means caring about the result and following it through. It does not mean doing everything yourself. A common mistake is stepping in and taking over when someone is struggling, which solves today's problem but weakens the person. Ask before you step in, for example, would it help if I took a look. And let others do it their way, as long as the outcome is met. Good leaders are comfortable with something done differently from how they would have done it. Ownership is about responsibility, not about control.

leadership-essentials.title: Lecture: Clarity beats charisma
leadership-essentials.text: A clear request has an outcome, an owner and a date Say less, and make it specific Check that it was understood. Many people believe leaders need charisma. In daily work, clarity matters far more. A clear request has three parts: the outcome you want, who owns it, and by when. Vague requests such as, can someone look at this, usually result in nothing, or in two people doing the same thing. Say less, and make it specific. Then check that it was understood, by asking the person to say in their own words what they will do. This takes thirty seconds and prevents days of confusion. Clear communication is a gift to the people around you.

leadership-essentials.title: Lecture: Communicating a clear next step
leadership-essentials.text: End every meeting with actions Write them down and share them Follow up on the date you agreed. One of the simplest leadership habits is to end every conversation with a clear next step. At the end of a meeting, summarise what was decided, who will do what, and by when. Write it down and share it the same day. Then follow up on the date you agreed, even if only with a quick message. This habit builds a reputation for reliability. People learn that when you are involved, things move. Many meetings fail not because of the discussion, but because nobody was sure what happened afterwards.

leadership-essentials.title: Lecture: Earning trust
leadership-essentials.text: Trust grows from small kept promises Do what you said you would do If you cannot, say so early. Trust is not built through big speeches. It grows from small kept promises. If you say you will send something by Friday, send it by Friday. If you say you will raise a concern with the manager, do it, and report back. When you cannot keep a promise, say so early and explain, instead of going quiet. People forgive missed deadlines far more easily than silence. Over time, a record of small kept promises becomes a reputation, and a reputation for being reliable is the foundation of leadership.

leadership-essentials.title: Lecture: Giving credit and taking responsibility
leadership-essentials.text: Share credit generously Take responsibility when things go wrong Learn out loud. Two habits mark out good leaders. They share credit generously, naming the people who did the work, in front of others. And they take responsibility when things go wrong, saying what they will do differently instead of pointing at others. Learning out loud, such as saying, I made a call that did not work, here is what I learned, shows others that mistakes are survivable. It makes it easier for everyone to be honest. Teams where credit is shared and responsibility is owned tend to be more open and more resilient.

leadership-essentials.title: Lecture: Listening as a leadership skill
leadership-essentials.text: Give full attention Ask a follow-up question Summarise before you respond. Listening is one of the most underrated leadership skills. Give people your full attention, which means putting your phone away. Ask a follow-up question that shows you want to understand more. And summarise what you heard before you respond. This simple habit slows the conversation down just enough to avoid misunderstandings. People who feel listened to are more willing to share problems early, and to support decisions even when they did not get their way. Leaders who listen well usually know what is actually going on.

leadership-essentials.title: Lecture: Your next steps
leadership-essentials.text: Use the outcome, owner, date format this week Keep one visible promise Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, use the outcome, owner and date format for every request you make this week. Choose one promise to keep visibly, and tell someone about it. Complete the workbook for this course, which includes a clear request template and a promise tracker. Then take the final quiz. When you reach the end of the last lesson you will receive your certificate and a personal review of how you worked through the course. Leadership starts with small, consistent behaviours, so start with one today.

leadership-essentials.title: Glossary: Ownership
leadership-essentials.text: Ownership: Taking responsibility for an outcome and following it through.

leadership-essentials.title: Glossary: Clear request
leadership-essentials.text: Clear request: A request that names the outcome, the owner and the date.

leadership-essentials.title: Glossary: Kept promise
leadership-essentials.text: Kept promise: A small commitment completed as agreed, or renegotiated early.

leadership-essentials.title: Glossary: Credit
leadership-essentials.text: Credit: Public recognition of the people who did the work.

leadership-essentials.title: Exercise: Clear request practice
leadership-essentials.text: Choose three requests you will make this week. Write each with an outcome, an owner and a date. Ask each person to repeat back what they will do. Note how many were completed on time.

leadership-essentials.title: Reflection questions
leadership-essentials.text: Where do you step in and take over when you could ask first? What request did you make recently that was not clear, and what happened? Which promise have you made that you have not yet kept?

team-foundations.title: Lecture: What great teams share
team-foundations.text: Psychological safety Clear goals and roles Reliable follow-through. Welcome to Team Foundations. Teams that work well tend to share three things. People feel safe to speak up, which is called psychological safety. The goals and roles are clear, so everybody knows what they are doing and why. And there is reliable follow-through, so when something is agreed, it happens. This lecture shows what each of those looks like on an ordinary day, and how any team member, not only the manager, can contribute to them. We will cover meetings, speaking up, and how to raise concerns early and kindly.

team-foundations.title: Lecture: What healthy teams look like day to day
team-foundations.text: People ask questions openly Disagreements are about the work Help is offered and accepted. In a healthy team, people ask questions without fear of looking foolish. Disagreements happen, but they stay about the work, not about people. Help is offered and accepted easily. Successes are shared and mistakes are discussed openly. None of this requires everyone to be best friends. It requires respect, and some habits that make respect visible. You can start those habits yourself. Thanking a colleague, asking a genuine question, or admitting a mistake all make it easier for others to do the same. Teams are shaped by what each person does.

team-foundations.title: Lecture: Meetings that matter
team-foundations.text: Prepare before you arrive Contribute, and make space for others Summarise and follow up. Meetings take up a lot of time, so it is worth making them useful. Prepare before you arrive, by reading the agenda and thinking about what you can add. During the meeting, contribute, and also make space for others, especially quieter colleagues. Ask, what do you think. At the end, summarise what was decided and who will do what. After the meeting, follow up in writing. Anyone can improve a meeting this way, whether or not they are leading it. A short, clear summary is often the most valued contribution in the room.

team-foundations.title: Lecture: Being a good contributor
team-foundations.text: Be on time and present Give ideas, not only problems Build on what others say. Good contributors are reliable and constructive. Be on time and be present, without checking your phone. When you raise a problem, try to bring an idea along with it. Build on what others say, using phrases like, yes, and we could also. This keeps momentum, and shows that you are listening. Avoid dismissing ideas too quickly, since the first version of an idea is rarely the best. Over time, people come to see you as someone who makes the group better, and that is a powerful reputation in any team.

team-foundations.title: Lecture: Speaking up
team-foundations.text: Decide what you want to say Be specific and calm Raise it early. Speaking up can feel risky, but silence has costs too. Before you speak, decide the one thing you want to say. Be specific, for example, I am worried the deadline does not allow time for testing. Keep your tone calm, and focus on the issue, not on a person. Raise it early, when there is still time to change course. If you are unsure, frame it as a question, such as, have we thought about how this affects the customer. Speaking up well is a skill, and it gets easier each time you do it.

team-foundations.title: Lecture: Responding when someone speaks up
team-foundations.text: Say thank you Ask a question before you answer Show what you will do with it. The other side of speaking up is how you respond when a colleague raises a concern. Start with thank you. Ask a question to understand it before you answer, such as, can you tell me more about what you are seeing. And show what you will do with the information, even if the answer is that you need time to think. If people raise concerns and nothing happens, they stop. If something happens, even something small, they keep going. How the team responds to the first concern decides whether there is a second.

team-foundations.title: Lecture: Handling disagreement kindly
team-foundations.text: Assume good intent Separate the idea from the person Look for what you agree on first. Disagreement is healthy when handled well. Assume good intent, which means thinking the other person is trying to help, until you see otherwise. Separate the idea from the person, by saying, I see it differently, rather than, you are wrong. Look for what you agree on first, because that gives you a base to work from. Ask what would change your mind, and what would change theirs. When a disagreement cannot be resolved, agree who decides, and then support the decision. Respect in disagreement builds trust faster than avoiding it.

team-foundations.title: Lecture: Your next steps
team-foundations.text: Add one thing to your next meeting Raise one small concern kindly Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, choose one thing that you will add to your next meeting, such as a summary of actions. Raise one small concern kindly, using the approach from this lecture. Complete the workbook for this course, which has a meeting checklist and a speaking up planner. Then take the final quiz. When you reach the end of the last lesson you will receive your certificate and a personal review of how you worked through the course. Teams improve one person's habit at a time, and you can start today.

team-foundations.title: Glossary: Psychological safety
team-foundations.text: Psychological safety: The belief that you can speak up without fear of embarrassment or punishment.

team-foundations.title: Glossary: Follow-through
team-foundations.text: Follow-through: Doing what was agreed, by the date it was agreed.

team-foundations.title: Glossary: Constructive
team-foundations.text: Constructive: Helping move something forward, for example by offering an idea alongside a problem.

team-foundations.title: Glossary: Good intent
team-foundations.text: Good intent: The assumption that a colleague is trying to help even when you disagree.

team-foundations.title: Exercise: Meeting contribution plan
team-foundations.text: Read the agenda and write one point you can add. Choose one quiet colleague and plan to ask for their view. Write a two-line summary of decisions at the end. Send it within a day.

team-foundations.title: Reflection questions
team-foundations.text: Which of the three shared traits of great teams is strongest in your team, and which is weakest? What stopped you the last time you wanted to speak up? How did your team respond the last time someone raised a concern?

high-performing-teams.title: Lecture: What holds teams back
high-performing-teams.text: Performance has causes you can find Most issues are trust, clarity or energy Diagnose before you fix. Welcome to Building High-Performing Teams. When a team underperforms, leaders often reach for a fix straight away, such as a new process or a team day out. But the cause may be something else. This lecture is about diagnosing first. Most team problems fall under trust, clarity or energy. Once you know which, the right action becomes obvious. We will cover how to run a quick team health check, how to design rituals that stick, and how to align several teams around shared goals, so that groups of teams work together instead of against each other.

high-performing-teams.title: Lecture: Diagnosing a team
high-performing-teams.text: Trust: do people speak openly Clarity: do they know goals and roles Energy: do they feel able to do good work. A quick diagnosis looks at three areas. Trust, which asks whether people speak openly and rely on each other. Clarity, which asks whether people know the goals, the roles and what good looks like. And energy, which asks whether people feel able to do good work, or whether they are stretched and tired. Ask short questions on each, using a simple scale. Do it anonymously, so that people are honest. The scores will not give you the full story, but they show where to look and where to start the conversation.

high-performing-teams.title: Lecture: Sharing results without blame
high-performing-teams.text: Share the scores openly Ask what stands out to the team Choose one thing to work on. Sharing the results is where many leaders go wrong. If the data feels like a judgement, people become defensive. Present the scores as information about the team, not about individuals. Ask the team what stands out to them, and what they would add. Listen more than you talk. Then choose one thing to work on, not five. A single, shared priority is more likely to move than a long list. Agree who will lead it and when you will review progress. The process of looking together often improves trust by itself.

high-performing-teams.title: Lecture: Rituals that stick
high-performing-teams.text: Small, regular and visible Tied to something that already happens Owned by the team, not only the leader. Most team agreements fade by Wednesday. Rituals help them last. A ritual is a small, regular action that the team does together, such as a short start of week check in, a Friday round of thanks, or a monthly look at what to stop doing. The best rituals are small, regular and visible. Tie them to something that already happens, such as an existing meeting. And make them owned by the team, so that they continue when the leader is away. Start with one ritual, and keep it going for two months before adding another.

high-performing-teams.title: Lecture: Designing a good ritual
high-performing-teams.text: Decide the purpose in one sentence Keep it under fifteen minutes Review whether it is still useful. To design a ritual, begin with the purpose in one sentence. For example, to make sure everyone knows the priorities for the week. Keep it under fifteen minutes, since long rituals get skipped. Rotate who leads it, so that the ownership is shared. And review every couple of months whether it is still useful. Drop it if not, because a ritual that has lost its point is worse than none. The aim is a small number of habits that people value, not a calendar full of obligations.

high-performing-teams.title: Lecture: Teams of teams
high-performing-teams.text: Shared goals across teams Clear interfaces between teams Leaders who connect rather than control. When several teams need to work together, new problems appear. Each team may optimise for its own goals, while the overall result suffers. To scale well, give the teams shared goals that they can all see. Make the interfaces between teams clear, meaning what each team provides to the others, and how to ask for it. And lead by connecting rather than controlling. Bring team leads together regularly, so that they hear each other's challenges. When teams understand each other's work, handovers improve, and conflict falls.

high-performing-teams.title: Lecture: Handling dependencies and handovers
high-performing-teams.text: Name dependencies early Agree what a good handover looks like Fix problems at the source. Many delays in larger organisations come from dependencies between teams. Name them early, in planning, rather than discovering them late. Agree what a good handover looks like, including what information is passed on and in what form. When something goes wrong, look for the cause at the source, rather than blaming the team where the problem showed up. A short regular meeting between teams that rely on each other can prevent months of friction. These are practical steps, but they make teams of teams feel like one organisation.

high-performing-teams.title: Lecture: Your next steps
high-performing-teams.text: Run a three-question health check Start one ritual for two months Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, run the three question health check with your team this month, and share the results openly. Choose one ritual to start, and commit to it for two months. Complete the workbook for this course, which has the health check form and a ritual design page. Then take the final quiz. When you reach the end of the last lesson you will receive your certificate and a personal review of how you worked through the course. High performance is built from steady habits, so begin with one and build from there.

high-performing-teams.title: Glossary: Team health check
high-performing-teams.text: Team health check: A short anonymous survey of trust, clarity and energy.

high-performing-teams.title: Glossary: Ritual
high-performing-teams.text: Ritual: A small, regular, visible team action that keeps an agreement alive.

high-performing-teams.title: Glossary: Dependency
high-performing-teams.text: Dependency: A piece of work that one team needs from another before it can proceed.

high-performing-teams.title: Glossary: Interface
high-performing-teams.text: Interface: The agreed way one team requests and receives work from another.

high-performing-teams.title: Exercise: Three-question health check
high-performing-teams.text: Write three questions on trust, clarity and energy, scored one to five. Collect the answers anonymously. Share the results and ask what stands out. Agree one action and an owner.

high-performing-teams.title: Reflection questions
high-performing-teams.text: Is your team's main constraint trust, clarity or energy, and how do you know? Which team ritual is already working, and what makes it stick? Which other team do you depend on most, and how clear is the handover?

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Lecture: Beyond the wellness app
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Perks rarely change outcomes Strain usually comes from work design Strategy starts with workload. Welcome to Well-being Strategy for Leaders. Many organisations respond to well-being concerns with perks, such as an app, a yoga class or a fruit bowl. These can be pleasant, but they rarely change how people feel about work. The biggest drivers of strain usually sit in how work is designed, including workload, control, clarity and relationships. This lecture covers how to link well-being to workload and the design of work, how to build a plan with real measures, and how to make support part of everyday management.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Lecture: What drives strain at work
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Workload and unrealistic deadlines Little control over how work is done Unclear roles and poor relationships. Research on workplace stress points to a few common drivers. Workload that is too high or deadlines that are unrealistic. Little control over how or when work is done. Unclear roles, so people are unsure what is expected. Poor relationships or a lack of support from managers. Change that is badly communicated also adds strain. Notice that most of these are about the way work is organised, not about individuals. That is good news, because leaders can change work design. A well-being strategy that ignores these drivers will struggle to make a difference.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Lecture: Linking well-being to workload
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Look at the real data on workload Ask where demands exceed capacity Change the work, not only the person. Start with the data you already have. Look at overtime, absence, project loads and deadlines. Ask where demands regularly exceed capacity, and why. Then change the work, not only the person. That might mean removing low-value tasks, extending a deadline, adding resource, or clarifying priorities. Teaching resilience is useful, but it should not replace fixing a workload that is unsustainable. When people see leaders act on workload, it builds trust in the whole well-being effort, because it shows that the concern leads to a real change.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Lecture: Measuring what matters
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Choose a handful of measures Combine data and pulse surveys Track change over time. A strategy needs measures, or it becomes a list of good intentions. Choose a handful, not dozens. Combine hard data, such as absence, turnover and overtime, with short pulse surveys that ask people how they feel. Track the same measures over time, so that you can see whether things are improving. Share the results with the people involved, and be honest when the numbers are not good. Be careful not to use the data to blame managers. The point of measuring is to learn where to act, and to check that what you did made a difference.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Lecture: Building a well-being plan
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: A clear owner and a small number of priorities Actions with dates A review every quarter. A good plan is short. It has a clear owner, a small number of priorities, and actions with dates. For example, reduce unplanned overtime in one department by a stated amount, or make sure every team has a regular conversation about workload. Link each priority to a measure, so you will know whether it worked. Review the plan every quarter. A plan that is written once and filed away has no effect. A plan that is visible and reviewed becomes part of how the organisation runs.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Lecture: Policy into practice
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Policies change nothing alone Give managers training and prompts Follow up on what happens. Policies are only words until managers apply them. A flexible working policy means little if managers quietly discourage it. To turn policy into practice, give managers training and simple prompts, such as a monthly question in one to ones about workload. Make it easy to find support, and easy to use. Then follow up on what actually happens, by asking whether managers are having these conversations, and what gets in the way. Leaders can help by doing it themselves, openly, since people copy what they see at the top.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Lecture: Making support part of everyday management
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Regular conversations, not crisis conversations Visible signposting Recognition of managers who do it well. The best support is built into everyday management, not reserved for a crisis. Encourage regular conversations about workload and energy in team meetings and one to ones. Make signposting visible, so that every employee knows what help exists and how to reach it. Recognise managers who handle these conversations well, since what gets recognised gets repeated. Over time, this shifts the culture, so that talking about well-being is normal, and asking for help is seen as sensible rather than as weakness.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Lecture: Your next steps
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Pick three measures to track Name one workload change to make Complete the workbook and the final quiz. To finish, choose three measures you will track, such as overtime, absence and a pulse score. Name one change to workload that you can make this quarter. Complete the workbook for this course, which has a plan template and a measures sheet. Then take the final quiz. When you reach the end of the last lesson you will receive your certificate and a personal review of how you worked through the course. A good strategy is practical and measured, so start small and review honestly.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Glossary: Work design
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Work design: How tasks, workload, control and roles are organised for a team or person.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Glossary: Pulse survey
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Pulse survey: A short, frequent survey that tracks how people are feeling.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Glossary: Signposting
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Signposting: Making it clear what support exists and how to reach it.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Glossary: Well-being plan
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Well-being plan: A short list of priorities, owners, actions and measures reviewed regularly.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Exercise: One-page well-being plan
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Write two priorities linked to workload. For each, name an owner, an action and a date. Choose one measure for each priority. Book the first quarterly review.

wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.title: Reflection questions
wellbeing-strategy-for-leaders.text: Which part of work design causes the most strain in your area? What data on workload could you look at this month? What happens when a manager in your organisation raises a workload concern?
